newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Uneximbank seen keeping Norilsk in the family.
newsitem.headline: Uneximbank seen keeping Norilsk in the family.

text.p: Russia's Uneximbank will probably keep its family jewel, a major stake in the giant Norilsk Nickel metals group, when the stake is offered through tender later this month, analysts said on Tuesday.

Uneximbank, one of Russia's most powerful commercial banks, plans to bid for its own stake -- a move analysts said would virtually guarantee it maintained control of one of the world's biggest base and precious metals producers.
"I think Uneximbank will definitely win the tender, there seems little doubt," said Tatyana Nikolskaya, analyst at Pioneer Securities in Moscow.
If Uneximbank keeps control of the 38 percent stake, which represents 51 percent of Norilsk's voting shares, it would have to continue to struggle with a cost-cutting programme at the company.
"It looks like being business as usual at Norilsk," said Julia Dawson, head of Russian equities research at ING Barings in London.

The government handed 38 percent of Norilsk to Uneximbank to manage in 1995 under its shares-for-loans scheme. The period over which the government could buy the stake back ran out on July 1, triggering the sale, which is set for July 22.

Uneximbank spokesman Sergei Chernitsyn said foreign investors would probably not be allowed to participate directly because the stake would be sold in a single lot exceeding the legal limit on foreign ownership in the company of 15 percent.
Analysts said a starting price of $117 million, plus $300 million in investment and payment of company debts worth $70 million, valued the sale at prices close to market levels.
The starting price plus additional payments "give a price per share of $10.02, which is in line with the average market price," CentreInvest Securities said in a market report.
Norilsk ordinary shares on the Russian Trading System traded at $11.75 on Tuesday afternoon, up from $11.37 late on Monday. Preferred shares rose sharply to $8.30 from Monday's close of $7.60.
The realistic price tag was rare for sales of shares used in shares-for-loans schemes, analysts said.
"This is about the only block of shares offered in the share-for-loans programme that is anywhere close to market value," said one analyst.

Dawson said holders of preferred shares would be big winners from the sale because Norilsk's charter states that when the 38 percent stake is sold, preferred shares would be converted into ordinaries, which are trading at a whopping 50 percent premium.
"Norilsk's preferred shares have been fairly liquid for that one reason," Dawson said.

CentreInvest said Uneximbank might declare it had already paid some of the required payments, lowering the price it would have to pay for the stake. "In this case we can assume that it (Uneximbank) would be the most likely winner," CentreInvest said.

Uneximbank has struggled to put together a rescue package to haul the Soviet-era mining monolith out of its debt crisis. Norilsk produces metals profitably, but huge social costs and hefty taxes have dragged it into the red.
Norilsk would benefit if Uneximbank maintained control after the sale, analysts said, because the bank had improved the management and financial control of the company.
Chernitsyn said the bank had succeeded in boosting Norilsk's share price, achieved regular payments by the group to various budgets and significantly boosted metals production.
The group produced nine percent more nickel in the first five months of 1997 than in the same year-ago period.
It has announced ambitious plans for the year, aiming to boost nickel output 20 percent to 213,000 tonnes, which would make it the world's biggest nickel firm by output.
But Norilsk officials have admitted that the target is only realistic if Moscow gives it debt and other relief.
